keyQuotes: AI can provide brilliant answers, but the ability to truly ask questions, maintain judgment, and build one's own narrative from fragments still belongs only to beings-in-the-world, who have desires, who hesitate, and who persist.
Life is a series of increasingly pure efforts.

AI is like a learned person who has never existed in history... In terms of creative advancement, there is nothing admirable about it. The questions AI raises are actually questions others have already asked.
The objectivity that historians pursue has little to do with their specific personal feelings... This is a starting point for historical research.

mainPoints.explanation: Chen Jiaying argues that living beings develop cognition because they have desires; cognition is not about receiving all information but about simplifying complexity. Objectivity is not a starting point but a process, akin to 'a series of increasingly pure efforts.'
mainPoints.point: Cognition stems from the desires of beings-in-the-world; objectivity is 'a series of increasingly pure efforts.'

mainPoints.explanation: Luo Xin points out that historical research pursues truth while being aware of its own limitations. Cultivating a sense of history, judgment, and the ability to ask questions is more important than reaching perfect conclusions; the process itself is education.
mainPoints.point: The greatest value of the humanities lies in the process, not in reaching a single conclusion.

mainPoints.explanation: Chen Jiaying believes that the way AI operates is fundamentally different from human cognition, though the results are highly similar. Luo Xin adds that AI is an 'extremely low-cost, interdisciplinary senior consultant' that can synthesize existing knowledge but cannot ask original questions like Chen Yinke could.
mainPoints.point: AI can mimic the results of cognition but cannot pose truly new questions.

mainPoints.explanation: The three scholars agree that AI can provide brilliant answers, but the ability to truly ask questions, maintain judgment, and build one's own narrative from fragments still belongs only to humans, and this ability can only be cultivated through humanistic training.
mainPoints.point: In the age of AI, the core value of philosophy and history is to cultivate judgment and narrative ability.

oneSentenceSummary: Three scholars, Chen Jiaying, Luo Xin, and Zhou Sicheng, engage in a dialogue on cognition, objectivity, and the value of the humanities in the age of AI, exploring how philosophy and history can help people build their own narratives and judgment amidst fragmented information.
originalTitle: 陈嘉映×罗新×周思成：谁在定义真实？
summary: This article is a transcript of a dialogue from the 2026 Utopia Reader's Day event. Chen Jiaying, from a philosophical perspective, explores the relationship between cognition and being-in-the-world, arguing that cognition stems from desire and can only be formed within specific contexts, with objectivity being 'a series of increasingly pure efforts.' Luo Xin responds from a historical viewpoint, emphasizing that historical research pursues truth while acknowledging its own limitations, and that the greatest value of the humanities lies in the process—cultivating judgment and the ability to ask questions. Zhou Sicheng raises the sharp question of whether AI can achieve 'the most objective cognition without being-in-the-world.' The three scholars agree that AI can provide brilliant answers and synthesize existing knowledge, but cannot truly pose new questions. In an era of AI as a 'deus ex machina,' the core value of philosophy and history lies in cultivating the human ability to ask questions, maintain judgment, and build one's own narrative from fragments. The dialogue also touches on the plurality of historical interpretation, the differences in objectivity between the social and natural sciences, and the shortcomings of Chinese education in terms of intellectual depth.
title: Chen Jiaying × Luo Xin × Zhou Sicheng: Who Defines Reality?
